subtopic_detail: Immediate advice on an established antiepileptic drug at first presentation in early pregnancy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends your general practice having done a positive home pregnancy test. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 3 days ago and the pregnancy was not planned.

She has generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy and has been free of seizures for 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily. Lamotrigine was stopped 6 years ago after a widespread rash requiring admission, and levetiracetam was stopped 5 years ago because of severe irritability and mood disturbance that resolved on withdrawal.

She has read about the risks of her medication overnight and has brought a printout. She is still taking the valproate and asks whether she should stop it today. She drives to work and cares for a 3-year-old niece two days a week. She takes no other medications and has not been taking folic acid.

data_table.History: Generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy, seizure free 4 years on sodium valproate 800 mg daily, previous severe rash on lamotrigine and severe mood disturbance on levetiracetam
data_table.Examination: Neurological examination normal, no focal deficit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate advice?

options.text: Halve the valproate dose today and arrange review at the joint clinic within 4 weeks
options.rationale: An abrupt halving of the dose risks breakthrough seizures without meaningfully reducing teratogenic risk at this gestation, since organogenesis of the neural tube is already complete. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Continue the valproate unchanged and arrange joint obstetric and neurology review this week
options.rationale: Neural tube closure is complete by about 6 weeks of gestation, so stopping valproate now cannot undo that risk, while abrupt withdrawal in a woman with generalised tonic-clonic seizures risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both of which are among the leading causes of maternal death in Australian reports. Any change of agent belongs to a specialist review arranged urgently, not to a single consultation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the valproate today, start folic acid 5 mg daily and review her again in 2 weeks
options.rationale: High-dose folic acid is indeed indicated and will be started, but coupling it with abrupt cessation of an effective anticonvulsant exposes her to seizure recurrence for no foetal benefit at 6 weeks. This is the most tempting option because half of it is correct. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Switch her to levetiracetam today at an equivalent dose and review her again in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is usually the preferred agent in pregnancy, but she has a documented history of severe mood disturbance on it, and any cross-taper in an established patient requires neurology supervision rather than a same-day switch. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Stop the valproate today and review the situation at her 12-week nuchal translucency scan
options.rationale: This combines abrupt withdrawal with a 6-week gap in supervision, which is the worst combination of seizure risk and lost opportunity to plan monitoring, foetal surveillance and delivery. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the commonly used antiepileptic drugs, with major congenital malformation rates around 10 per cent and a dose-dependent risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and it should be avoided in women of childbearing potential wherever an alternative works. The clinical problem in this consultation is different: the exposure has already occurred and the neural tube closed weeks ago, so the decision is about seizure safety from here on. Uncontrolled generalised tonic-clonic seizures in pregnancy carry risks of maternal trauma, foetal hypoxia, status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, and epilepsy consistently features among indirect causes of maternal death in Australian and United Kingdom mortality reports. Management therefore centres on urgent specialist review, high-dose folic acid, a detailed anomaly scan, monitoring of drug levels across pregnancy, and planning for the postnatal period including vitamin K and safe infant care advice.
key_points: Neural tube closure completes by about 6 weeks, so stopping valproate at that point does not reverse the risk already incurred
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, both recognised causes of maternal death
Start folic acid 5 mg daily and refer urgently to a joint obstetric and neurology clinic
Arrange a detailed anomaly scan and monitor antiepileptic levels, which fall across pregnancy
Any change of agent is made by the specialist team with a supervised cross-taper, not same day in general practice
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine plasma concentrations can fall by more than half by the third trimester because of oestrogen-driven glucuronidation, so levels are checked each trimester and the dose is reduced again within 2 weeks of birth to avoid toxicity.

subtopic_detail: Selecting heart failure therapy in the early postpartum period while breastfeeding is continuing
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar asked to review a 33-year-old woman on day 5 after a normal vaginal birth of her third baby.

She was readmitted overnight with breathlessness lying flat and waking gasping at 2 am. She has no pleuritic pain, no calf swelling and no cough. She had no hypertension in pregnancy and no proteinuria at any visit.

Her chest radiograph shows upper lobe venous diversion with small effusions, and a computed tomography pulmonary angiogram performed overnight excludes pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiography today reports a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 32 per cent and no valvular lesion. Her N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide is 4100 ng/L (below 125) and her troponin is within normal limits. She is breastfeeding fully and is very keen to continue. The intern has charted frusemide and asks you what else to start.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 104/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Elevated jugular venous pressure, bibasal crackles, mild ankle oedema, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide 4100 ng/L (below 125), troponin within normal limits, creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2)
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph with upper lobe venous diversion and small effusions; computed tomography pulmonary angiogram negative for embolism; echocardiogram dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 32 per cent and no valvular lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate addition to her frusemide?

options.text: Digoxin with ongoing frusemide, deferring other agents until an echocardiogram in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Digoxin is compatible with breastfeeding and may help rate control, but it does not modify remodelling, and deferring disease-modifying therapy for 6 weeks wastes the period in which recovery is most achievable. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Candesartan with spironolactone, advising her to suppress lactation and switch to formula
options.rationale: Angiotensin receptor blockers lack the breastfeeding safety data that older angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors have, and there is no need to stop breastfeeding when compatible alternatives exist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Sacubitril with valsartan and cabergoline to suppress lactation, with frusemide continued
options.rationale: Sacubitril with valsartan has no safety data in lactation and is not a first-line initiation agent in the puerperium, and routine lactation suppression is not required; cabergoline in peripartum cardiomyopathy remains an investigational adjunct rather than standard care. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Enalapril with metoprolol, continuing frusemide and supporting her to keep breastfeeding
options.rationale: Once the baby is born the teratogenic objection to renin-angiotensin blockade no longer applies, and enalapril and captopril are the angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors with the best data in lactation, passing into milk in negligible amounts. Adding a beta blocker completes the two agents that drive reverse remodelling, and recovery of ejection fraction in peripartum cardiomyopathy is best when therapy starts early. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

options.text: Frusemide alone at a higher dose, avoiding all other agents for as long as she is breastfeeding
options.rationale: This reflects the common misconception that lactation blocks all heart failure therapy; diuresis relieves congestion but leaves the ventricle without any remodelling therapy during the window when recovery is most likely. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

explanation.summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is heart failure with reduced ejection fraction arising in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum without another identifiable cause, and it is a leading cardiac contributor to maternal mortality in Australia. Orthopnoea and waking gasping distinguish it from the ordinary breathlessness of late pregnancy and the early puerperium, and natriuretic peptide is a useful discriminator because it stays near normal in physiological breathlessness. Treatment after birth follows standard heart failure principles, with drug choice adjusted for lactation rather than abandoned because of it: enalapril, captopril, metoprolol, frusemide and hydralazine with nitrate are all usable. Anticoagulation is considered when the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, because the puerperium is already prothrombotic and mural thrombus is well described. Contraception counselling is essential, since a subsequent pregnancy carries a significant risk of relapse, particularly if ventricular function has not normalised.
key_points: Peripartum cardiomyopathy arises in the last month of pregnancy or the first 5 months postpartum with no other cause
After birth, enalapril and captopril are the preferred angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors during breastfeeding
Beta blockade with metoprolol is added for reverse remodelling; frusemide treats congestion only
Consider anticoagulation where the ejection fraction is markedly reduced, given puerperal thrombotic risk
Counsel about contraception and the risk of relapse in a future pregnancy, especially if function does not normalise
explanation.pearls: Bromocriptine added to standard therapy has been studied in peripartum cardiomyopathy on the basis of the prolactin fragment hypothesis, but it requires lactation suppression and anticoagulation cover and is not routine Australian practice.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Heart failure guidelines

subtopic_detail: First trimester anticoagulation choice for a mechanical mitral valve on a low warfarin dose
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic. A 31-year-old woman attends at 6 weeks in an unplanned first pregnancy.

She had rheumatic fever as a child in the Pacific and underwent mitral valve replacement with a bileaflet mechanical prosthesis 7 years ago. She takes warfarin 3 mg daily with a target international normalised ratio of 3.0 and has had no thromboembolic or bleeding events since surgery.

Her international normalised ratio today is 2.9 and her renal and liver function are normal. Echocardiography 3 months ago showed a normally functioning prosthesis with no regurgitation and normal ventricular function. She is in sinus rhythm. She is very anxious about the reports she has read about warfarin and asks whether she should be changed to injections for the rest of the pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Mechanical first heart sound, no murmur of prosthetic dysfunction, sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.9 on warfarin 3 mg daily, renal and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Echocardiogram 3 months ago with normally functioning bileaflet mitral prosthesis and normal ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan for the first trimester?

options.text: Stop warfarin and use aspirin 100 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone is grossly inadequate for a mechanical mitral prosthesis and would expose her to a high risk of valve thrombosis, which carries substantial maternal and foetal mortality. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Stop warfarin and use rivaroxaban 20 mg daily until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves in any patient after trials showed excess thromboembolism and bleeding, and they are separately contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue warfarin at her current dose with weekly international normalised ratio monitoring
options.rationale: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and falls to around 3 per cent or less at doses of 5 mg daily or under, so at 3 mg daily continuation offers the lowest maternal risk of valve thrombosis for a small foetal risk, and this is the recommended strategy for low-dose warfarin. Weekly monitoring accounts for the shifting warfarin requirement across pregnancy, and the switch to heparin is planned near term rather than now. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Stop warfarin and use therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily until 12 weeks, then resume warfarin
options.rationale: Substituting low molecular weight heparin through the first trimester avoids embryopathy but carries a higher rate of valve thrombosis, and it is the preferred strategy only when the warfarin dose needed exceeds 5 mg daily or the woman declines warfarin after counselling. This is the genuine near-pair, separated by the warfarin dose threshold. (Source: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease)
source_refs: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

options.text: Admit her for an unfractionated heparin infusion until 12 weeks, then resume her warfarin
options.rationale: An intravenous infusion for 6 weeks is impractical and carries risks of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, osteoporosis and line infection, and unfractionated heparin is reserved for the peripartum period when rapid reversibility matters. (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac disease in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation for a mechanical heart valve in pregnancy is one of the clearest examples of a decision that trades maternal against foetal risk, and no option is free of harm. Warfarin gives the best protection against valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes embryopathy, with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses, when exposure occurs between 6 and 12 weeks. That risk is strongly dose dependent, which is why the 5 mg daily threshold has become the pivot of the decision: at or below it, continuation is recommended, and above it, a first trimester switch to therapeutic low molecular weight heparin with anti-Xa monitoring is offered. Warfarin is stopped and replaced with heparin from around 36 weeks so that the foetus is not anticoagulated at delivery, since foetal liver immaturity means the foetal international normalised ratio exceeds the maternal one. Care belongs in a joint cardiac obstetric clinic in a centre with cardiac surgical backup.
key_points: The warfarin dose threshold of 5 mg daily decides whether to continue warfarin or switch in the first trimester
Embryopathy risk is concentrated in exposure between 6 and 12 weeks and is dose dependent
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves and in pregnancy
Switch to heparin at around 36 weeks so the foetus is not anticoagulated at birth
Valve thrombosis carries high maternal and foetal mortality, which is why heparin strategies are not automatically safer
explanation.pearls: Monitor therapeutic low molecular weight heparin in mechanical valve pregnancies with peak anti-Xa levels 4 to 6 hours after a dose, targeting about 1.0 to 1.2 IU/mL, since weight-based dosing alone is unreliable as pregnancy alters clearance.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand: Position statement on valvular heart disease

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a negative oestrogen and progestogen challenge in secondary amenorrhoea after uterine instrumentation
stem:
A 31-year-old woman is referred to your gynaecology clinic because she has had no periods for 11 months and has been unable to conceive.

Fourteen months ago she had a surgical evacuation of retained products of conception for secondary postpartum bleeding, which was repeated a week later for persistent bleeding. She breastfed for 3 months and stopped 10 months ago. Her periods have never returned.

She has no hot flushes, no night sweats and no vaginal dryness. Her weight is stable and her exercise and eating patterns are unchanged. She has no headache, no galactorrhoea and no visual symptoms, and she takes no medication.

Her pregnancy test is negative. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone is 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol is 340 pmol/L, prolactin is 290 mIU/L and thyroid stimulating hormone is 1.6 mIU/L, all within the reference range for the follicular phase. She bled neither after a 10-day course of medroxyprogesterone acetate nor after a subsequent 21-day cycle of oestrogen followed by progestogen. Transvaginal ultrasound reports a thin irregular endometrial line with bright echogenic areas.

data_table.Examination: Normal secondary sexual characteristics, normal external genitalia and cervix, no galactorrhoea
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol 340 pmol/L, prolactin 290 mIU/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.6 mIU/L, all within the follicular phase reference range; pregnancy test negative
data_table.Challenge testing: No withdrawal bleed after 10 days of medroxyprogesterone acetate; no bleed after a subsequent 21-day oestrogen and progestogen cycle
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound with a thin irregular endometrial line and bright echogenic areas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange diagnostic hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis under direct vision
options.rationale: Ovulatory hormone levels with a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge locate the problem in the outflow tract rather than the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, and repeated instrumentation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions. Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment, since adhesions are divided under direct vision. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.text: Request an anti-Mullerian hormone level and repeat follicle stimulating hormone in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Ovarian reserve testing investigates premature ovarian insufficiency, which is excluded here by a normal follicle stimulating hormone and a clearly normal oestradiol, alongside the absence of any vasomotor symptoms. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa to exclude a pituitary lesion
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging is indicated with a raised prolactin, headache, visual field loss or hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, none of which is present; her gonadotrophins and oestradiol confirm an intact axis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a combined oral contraceptive pill to re-establish a regular withdrawal bleed pattern
options.rationale: This would provide exogenous hormone to an endometrium that has already failed to respond to a formal oestrogen and progestogen challenge, and it also frustrates her stated wish to conceive. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

options.text: Measure a 17-hydroxyprogesterone level and free androgen index for an androgen excess disorder
options.rationale: Androgen excess evaluation belongs to women with hirsutism, acne or a raised luteinising hormone to follicle stimulating hormone ratio, and it would not explain a failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge whatever the result. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea investigation and management)

explanation.summary: Secondary amenorrhoea is worked through by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary and hypothalamus. The progestogen challenge tests whether an oestrogenised endometrium and a patent outflow tract are present, and a negative result is followed by an oestrogen and progestogen challenge to separate an unresponsive endometrium from simple anovulation. Failure of both challenges in a woman with normal gonadotrophins and normal oestradiol points to the endometrium or the outflow tract, and intrauterine adhesions are the dominant cause when there has been recent uterine instrumentation, particularly repeated evacuation of a puerperal uterus or curettage in the presence of infection. Ultrasound may show a thin irregular endometrium with echogenic areas but cannot exclude adhesions, so hysteroscopy remains the definitive test. Treatment is hysteroscopic adhesiolysis, often with measures to prevent re-adhesion, and fertility outcomes depend heavily on the severity of disease at the time of diagnosis.
key_points: Work through secondary amenorrhoea by compartment: outflow tract, ovary, pituitary, hypothalamus
A failed oestrogen and progestogen challenge with normal gonadotrophins localises the problem to the endometrium or outflow tract
Repeated evacuation of a recently pregnant uterus is the classic antecedent of intrauterine adhesions
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment; ultrasound cannot exclude adhesions
Normal oestradiol with no vasomotor symptoms argues strongly against premature ovarian insufficiency
explanation.pearls: The risk of adhesions rises sharply when evacuation is performed on a postpartum or post-miscarriage uterus rather than a non-pregnant one, and repeat procedures within a fortnight carry the highest risk of all; this is a specific argument for expectant or medical management of retained products where it is safe.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Amenorrhoea clinical guideline

subtopic_detail: First line treatment for a chronic tic disorder causing social impairment in a school aged child
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a child and adolescent mental health service. A 9-year-old boy is referred by his general practitioner because of 18 months of repeated eye blinking and sideways head jerking, joined 6 months ago by repeated throat clearing.

His mother says the movements are worse when he is tired or anxious and almost disappear when he is absorbed in building models. He tells you he can hold them in for a while at school but then has to let them out in a rush when he gets home.

He has no injuries from the movements. He has no repetitive hand washing, no checking and no intrusive thoughts, and his teacher reports he concentrates well and his marks are at year level. He is being mimicked in the playground and has started asking to stay home. Neurological examination is normal and he takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: Frequent eye blinking and head jerking with throat clearing, suppressible for short periods, normal neurological examination
data_table.Collateral: Teacher reports concentration at year level and marks at year level; peers mimicking him at school

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Start clonidine at a low night-time dose and titrate it over the following 6 weeks
options.rationale: Clonidine is a reasonable pharmacological choice, particularly where attention deficit hyperactivity disorder coexists, but medication sits behind behavioural therapy in the treatment sequence for tics of this severity. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.text: Start aripiprazole at a low daily dose and review his movements in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Aripiprazole has the best evidence among antipsychotics for tic reduction, but exposing a 9-year-old to metabolic and extrapyramidal risk before trying behavioural therapy inverts the recommended order. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.text: Start risperidone at a low night-time dose and review his movements in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone reduces tics but carries the highest prolactin elevation and weight gain burden of the commonly used agents in children, so it is a later choice rather than a first line one. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.text: Provide reassurance about the natural history alone and review him again in 12 months
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is right for tics that cause no impairment, but he is being mimicked at school and is now avoiding it, which is functional impairment and an indication to treat. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

options.text: Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics with a trained therapist
options.rationale: Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics combines awareness training, a competing response and functional strategies, and it has the strongest evidence base of any first line treatment with none of the pharmacological burden. The suppressibility and build-up of urge he describes are exactly the premonitory phenomena the therapy works on. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect around 1 per cent of school aged children and typically begin between 5 and 7 years, peak in severity around 10 to 12 years, and improve substantially through adolescence. The decision to treat rests on functional impairment rather than on tic frequency, since many children with visible tics need nothing more than education for the family and the school. Behavioural therapy is first line worldwide, and Australian practice follows that order, with medication added when therapy is unavailable or insufficient. Coexisting conditions drive much of the disability: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder are each present in a substantial minority and should be actively screened for. Where medication is needed, alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and antipsychotics such as aripiprazole are the main options, chosen partly by which comorbidity is present.
key_points: Treat on functional impairment, not on tic count or visibility
Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first line, using awareness training and a competing response
Screen for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder, which drive much of the impairment
Clonidine and aripiprazole are the main pharmacological options when therapy is insufficient or unavailable
Tics usually peak around 10 to 12 years and improve substantially by late adolescence
explanation.pearls: The premonitory urge, an uncomfortable build-up relieved by performing the tic, is what separates tics from other movement disorders and is the specific target of the competing response in behavioural therapy.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for tic disorders
